messages.subject: Re: Data do not pass through sourced R scripts in map phase, but OK in reduce phase
messages.subject_clean: Data do not pass through sourced R scripts in map phase, but OK in reduce phase
messages.body_plain:
What is happening here is this:  "b <- .5" is inside a map expression. The Map expression does not get evaluated in the R global environment; however, "source" by defaults evaluates into the R global environment.  I believe the user work around is to do source(..., local=TRUE)

It may be possible to make Rhipe respond to this issue, but I am  not sure about the side effects of doing so at the moment.

The map expression is evaluated by this line in the source:

https://github.com/saptarshiguha/RHIPE/blob/master/code/R/src/mapreduce.cc#L266
Note the second argument to R_tryEval is NULL and it is the environment in which to evaluate Map expressions.  For comparison tryEval is basically the same as the eval documented here (but with a try logic)
http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Evaluating-R-expressions-from-C

If desired it is possible to evaluate the Map expressions in the global environment by changing the second argument in line 266.  For example like that demonstrated here:
http://developer.r-project.org/embedded.html

R_tryEval(runner2,R_GlobalEnv,&Rerr);

That would make Map expression evaluations and source(...,local=FALSE) creating variables in the same environment.

messages.subject: Google Protocol Buffer the whole MapReduce communication
messages.subject_clean: Google Protocol Buffer the whole MapReduce communication
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It occurred to me that if there is ever a rewrite of the internals of Rhipe that we should Google Protocol Buffer the whole communication between Java and C via pipes.

Right now the role of Google Protocol Buffers is to define the serialization of key value pairs via rexp.proto.  rexp.proto gets used in both the storage on the HDFS (map/sequence) and in the pipe data transfer from the Java MapReduce process to the RhipeMapReduce C program.

Inside of the communication between the Java and the C program is an ad hoc message format parsed in C here:
https://github.com/saptarshiguha/RHIPE/blob/master/code/R/src/mapreduce.cc#L79

As you can the message format starts with a 64 bit integer.  That integer is either the number of bytes to read or if a negative integer it is a MapReduce "message" indicating the status of the Map or Reduce (ie  Map Setup, Mapping, Reduce Setup etc).  There is really no reason to be doing that work "by-hand" if we are already depending on protobuf.  One can imagine writing another mapreduce.proto that defines the messages and  buffers of rexp.proto as necessary.

This would have the advantage of clear documentation of Java and C communication , automatic generation of parsing classes from C and Java, and  perhaps make easier future changes to the communication between Java and C, while also making one of the messiest pieces of code easier to read.  I wonder if it would even do away with all the big-indian little-indian parsing issues that are buried in the C code (perhaps indicating that the result is more portable too since we have offloaded the C and Java communication to Google classes?)

It isn't actually a hard change.  It is just a change that touches on everything Rhipe does so it is high risk.

messages.subject: rhfmt feedback
messages.subject_clean: rhfmt feedback
messages.body_plain:
I am converting my test cases to the new demands of Rhipe .73.  You have been busy.

I wanted to give some feedback on rhfmt:

> rhfmt("test", "text")
Error in match(x, table, nomatch = 0L) :
  argument "type" is missing, with no default

The formals of rhfmt are function(..., type).

By putting the ... in front of type you make it impossible to use argument order based calls to rhfmt.  As a general matter of R style I think people put "..." at the end to avoid that.

If it gets changed to rhfmt(type, ...) then you can still use the same call as you have been using:

rhfmt("path/to", type="text")

and the "path/to" will get matched to the "...".  So there is no change to existing code.

It is just that now people can also do

rhfmt("text", "path/to") if they should so desire.

To be clear there are currently two types of communication between processes in Rhipe:
Pass by environmental variable
Pass by buffer

I was just thinking about the pass by buffer situation as it is the easiest target for Google Protocol Buffer replacement. In retrospect the environmental variables could be done away with too (more later).

I cooked up a prototype .proto file here: https://gist.github.com/jrounds/5522736  This file passes a build through "protoc" but hasn't been dropped into code yet.

It is meant to be a drop in replacement of Rhipes ad hoc pipe communication rather then a re-imagining of Rhipe's engineering.

The key messages are "FromHadoopMapReduce" and "ToHadoopMapReduce".

The FromHadoopMapReduce contains a state (required) which you designed and then "optional" and "repeated" RExp or Rexp Key, value pairs depending on state. So here already is one thing made easier: We have off loaded the reading of entire buffers of repeated values to Google.

So the pseudo-code is something like
MapReduce Engine in C:
  read first FromHadoopMapReduce message using bool ParseFromIstream(istream* input);
  dispatch to function corresponding to message.state
  evaluate whether ToHadoopMapReduce message needs to be pushed to Java yet via SerializeToOstream(&output)

The dispatch functions would be like:
int map_setup(FromHadoopMapReduce message);
int map_map(FromHadoopMapReduce message);
int map_cleanup(FromHadoopMapReduce message);
int reduce_pre(FromHadoopMapReduce message);

etc.

I would just use global variables between dispatches of MapReduce engine to keep it simple.  For example, https://github.com/saptarshiguha/RHIPE/blob/master/code/R/src/mapreduce.cc#L205 mainMapperLoop has several buffer variables it needs.   Just g_ them and make them global.  You don't want static because you want map_setup to be able to initialize them.

example pseudo-code for one particular function:

map_map (FromHadoopMapReduce* message):
   Rexp KV to Sexp KV (message->map_data, g_sexp_buffers)
   do Rf_setvars from g_sexp_buffers
   do Rf_eval of map expression
   push to combiner buffer if combining push to global gp_ToHadoopMapReduce->data if not
   check to see if combiner needs to execute
   return

The design of FromHadoopMapReduce is so close to your design that the code would write easily.  I am willing to do it, I just need to know someone else cares, and someone else will help me validate that it is correct.

Thanks

> > > It occurred to me that if there is ever a rewrite of the internals of Rhipe that we should Google Protocol Buffer the whole communication between Java and C via pipes.
> > >
> > >
> > > Right now the role of Google Protocol Buffers is to define the serialization of key value pairs via rexp.proto.  rexp.proto gets used in both the storage on the HDFS (map/sequence) and in the pipe data transfer from the Java MapReduce process to the RhipeMapReduce C program.
> > >
> > > Inside of the communication between the Java and the C program is an ad hoc message format parsed in C here:
> > > https://github.com/saptarshiguha/RHIPE/blob/master/code/R/src/mapreduce.cc#L79
> > >
> > > As you can the message format starts with a 64 bit integer.  That integer is either the number of bytes to read or if a negative integer it is a MapReduce "message" indicating the status of the Map or Reduce (ie  Map Setup, Mapping, Reduce Setup etc).  There is really no reason to be doing that work "by-hand" if we are already depending on protobuf.  One can imagine writing another mapreduce.proto that defines the messages and  buffers of rexp.proto as necessary.
> > >
> > >
> > > This would have the advantage of clear documentation of Java and C communication , automatic generation of parsing classes from C and Java, and  perhaps make easier future changes to the communication between Java and C, while also making one of the messiest pieces of code easier to read.  I wonder if it would even do away with all the big-indian little-indian parsing issues that are buried in the C code (perhaps indicating that the result is more portable too since we have offloaded the C and Java communication to Google classes?)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > It isn't actually a hard change.  It is just a change that touches on everything Rhipe does so it is high risk.

Read 10 objects(13.76 MB) in 12.69 seconds

You can see there is a small disagreement about how long the read takes.  91 is right.

  4.924  15.396  78.061

For example, x above from the trivial rhwatch has

There are a total of 1654 part-r directories for this map file input.

Going forward it may be required to think about how to scan this directory the least amount possible.  Also, the design of map files (with the extra) directory versus sequence files seems to contribute to this problem.  With the advent of rhipe file objects it seems conceivable to scan a map file directory exactly once per an R sessions instead of every single time a rhread or rhwatch is done.

Full disclosure: this isn't actually a HDFS.  It is lustre storage on high capacity network fabricate.

messages.subject: Random thought about Hive
messages.subject_clean: Random thought about Hive
messages.body_plain:
Hi random thought about Hive,

Not to be assumed as a promise to do anything.

We have been thinking lately about how to export data out of Rhipe into a data format that supports structured queries (SQL-like) for external collaboration.  Basically data comes into the Rhipe framework gets processes and goes out to other scientist who don't use hadoop.  We are torn as nothing seems "right sized".  The big problem is the data we want to export can be in the TB size, and propagating it into another technology via MapReduces requires concurrent writes, but none of the concurrent write data base technologies are something we want to support or really even have the expertise to be getting involved in.

So I was thinking about Hive today which I think of as something in the middle.  Hive at least exposes an interface where non-hadoop scientist can write a query which gets translated into MapReduce and get data out.  It is not a particularly speedy sounding solution, but at least it takes the Rhipe writing analyst out of the loop for writing custom MapReduces to get the same data.

Why the post though?

I was looking at this post:
http://www.nearinfinity.com/blogs/stephen_mouring_jr/2013/01/04/writing-hive-tables-from-mapreduce.html

Where the author points out that a MapReduce can read and write hive tables.  Which I thought was interesting because they didn't look all that complicated.   The data format that hive can handle is not as unstructured and expressive as a Rhipe, but if one steps back one can imagine a java class that takes rhcollect(NULL, matrix/data.frame) and translates it into hive format and vice-versa.   Potentially you could even jump back into a hive export, do your science with Rhipe, and jump back out with  a hive format output. i.e (input= rhfmt(..., type="hive", output=rhfmt(...,type="hive").  Thing is though the author points out that there is a step after the MapReduce where you have to tell hive about the update to a table, so I am not sure how practical that is if not used very carefully.

I think it might be handy for that "jumping off" point where you leave the Rhipe pipe, and need to hand off to someone else.

Obviously, I don't expect you to implement this, I was just brainstorming.

Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: [rhipe] High execution time and Combiner usage
messages.subject_clean: [rhipe] High execution time and Combiner usage
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The concept of Reduce(also called Fold) as been present since the dawn of
CS. Google/Hadoop's MapReduce  takes this to a distributed level (and quite a
marvel it is).

The map function sends as output values tagged by keys. No function is applied
to the values. However the keys are 'partitioned'. As an example, consider
integer keys and mapred.reduce.tasks(R) set to 100. Then the partitioner function
is applied to these integer keys

Partitioner(key) = key modulo R

Thus however many distinct integer keys the map produces, each emitted key/value
pair get's assigned to one of the R reducers. That is, all emitted KV pairs with
Partitioner(key) equal to 0 modulo R is assigned to one reducer. If the map
outputs a million records, these records get assigned to 100 different buckets
(not necessarily equally distributed across the R buckets, that depends on the
key distribution).

So far the reducer is an abstract concept. All the values that share the same
exact key get "Reduced". If a cluster Rc computers, these R buckets are assigned
to the Rc computers.

Now the reduce begins. Let {V1,V2,...,Vn} be the values emitted by the map that
share the same _exact_ key. If you read the Wikipedia page for Reduce/Fold,
let's called the function F, then the output is (for a left reduce)

F(...F(F(F(startValue,V1),V2),V3))

That is take a startValue, apply F to that and the first incoming value, then
take the output and F to that and next value and so on.

So a sum, i.e. 2+3+4+5+...+n is essentially

Sum(Sum(Sum(  Sum(0,2) , 3),4),....) and so on.

Consider the 'min'

Min(Min(Min(Inf,2),3),4)....

and so on.

How does this look in the Java version of the Reduce, see [1],

   public void reduce(Key key, Iterable values,...)
     int sum = 0;
     for (IntWritable val : values) {
       sum += val.get();
     }
     send output to hadoop
   }

That is sum is initialized to 0, then sum is added to the first value, then this
sum is added to the next value.

And that is the Reduce of MapReduce. You might already know this. Note if
operations (e.g. sum/min) are commutative (order doesn't matter) and associative
(arrangement doesn't matter), then you can perform the Reduce on _subsets_ of
the values (sharing the same exact key). Having computed the Reduce on the
subsets we have Foutput1, Foutput2,.... Then the Reduce is applied to Foutput1,
Foutput2, and so on. Consider the sum

2+3+4+5+6+7

is same as (2+3)  + (5+7) + (4+6) (arrangement/order dont matter)
So the reduce is computed on {2,3}, {5,7} and {4,6} (the combiner is doing these
in the map phase). The outputs of these mini reduces are sent to the final
Reduce stage, and the Reduce function reduces {5, 12, 10} to get the final
answer.

If your operations are assoc/commutative, _use_ a combiner!

The R version
-------------

If i had to map R exactly the same way as Java, then rhwatch would take the
following function in reduce parameter

reduce=expression({
        sum  = 0                            ## 1.We got a reduce key
        while(TRUE){
          sum = sum+get.next.reduce.value() ## 2.keep looping to get all values for the key
          if (!has.more.reduce.values?())
            break
        }
                                            ## 3.Done with all reduce values, now write to disk
        rhcollect(reduce.key, sum)
        })

This is *costly* because i have to call a function for _every_ reduce value! In
R, as you might be well aware, if you want performance, you need to vectorize.

So the above now looks like

reduce = expression(
       ## 1. Pre is called _once_ for every reduce key
       pre = { .sum = 0},

       ## 2. 'reduce' is called  several times, each time reduce.values is a _list_ of the values
       ##    emitted from 'map' (or 'reduce' if a combiner is being used)
       reduce = { .sum = .sum + sum(unlist(reduce.values)) },

       ## 3. 'post' is called when _all_ reduce values have been processed (even
       ##    in a combiner). Unless you are _positive_ that "reduce" will only be
       ##    called once, rhcollect should _only_ appear here

       post = { rhcollect(reduce.key, .sum)}
       )

Since a sum is commutative and associative, i can use a combiner here. If one
uses the combiner, then the output from the map (the 'shape') should be the same
as the shape from the reduce expression above. This is because, one subsets of
the map output (again sharing the same key), the above reduce expressions are
called. When the map is complete, this output is shuffled,sorted and sent to the
reduce.

Thus the reduce expressions are called _again_ on the output it returned in
map/combiner stage.

For another example, my input data set has

userID, timestamp, x

I want to keep the first 1000 rows for each userID sorted by time(e.g. the first
1000 calls).

map = expression({
  rhcollect(userID, data.frame( userid=userid, ts=timestamp, x=x))
  })
NUM = 1000
reduce = expression(
   pre = { dfkeep = NULL },
   reduce = {
          ## reduce.values is a list of shape list( userid=userid, ts=timestamp, x=x)
          ## where userid is the same for every element in the list, since
          ## userid is the key
          dfkeep = rbind(dfkeep, do.call(rbind, reduce.values))
          dfkeep = head(df[order(df$ts),],NUM)
          },
   post = { rhcollect(reduce.key, dfkeep) }
   )

(* data frames are conceptually easier, for performance one might use lists,
though the code is more complicated)

The above code can be used with a combiner, since the essential operation is a
'min'. When the reduce gets a new user id, dfkeep is assigned to NULL. The
'reduce$reduce' is called with a list of  list( userid=userid, ts=timestamp,
x=x), which are rbinded into one big data frame. The first NUM obs are kept and
in 'post' written out.  If no combiner were used, then _all_ the values for the
userid would be sent to one reduce computer, the reduce$reduce would be called
repeatedly. This is wasteful. Instead by using a combiner, the above is called
on subsets of the rows (corresponding to the same user id).

If one uses a combiner, it _sometimes_ useful to have different operations
depending on whether the above reduce code is called in the combine stage or the
reduce stage. The main difference is that when the code is called in the reduce
stage, the rhcollect sends data to the final output folder. When the above code
is called in the Combine stage, the output is sent to the Reducer.

In the reduce expression, to know if the code is being called in the Combine
mode .rhipe.current.state is set to 'map.combine'. When the reduce code is being
called in the final Reduce stage(of the MapReduce dance), then
.rhipe.current.state is set to 'reduce'. I dont encourage using these variables
- it makes code confusing.

Lastly, the biggest hit in the reduce (in it's current implementation) is when
you have billions of unique keys, each with a handful of values. The the
reduce$pre, reduce$reduce,reduce$post invocation sequence becomes costlier than
the actual useful execution time. I haven't come up with a good way to get
around this (assuming the user doesn't make any guarantees)

I hope this helps. Feel free to ask questions. if you can produce reproducible
code, that helps too.

Regards
Saptarshi

I and Ryan, have consided using RCFile or some sort of blocked columnar storage (take a look at Trevni)
as a custom format for RHIPE based data analysis.

need coders := interested people who can code in Java(possibly C) and R (good/idiomatic R)

On Tue, May 21, 2013 at 11:40 AM, Jeremiah Rounds <roundsj...@gmail.com> wrote:

> A collaborator pointed out RCFile to me http://hive.apache.org/docs/r0.9.0/api/org/apache/hadoop/hive/ql/io/RCFile.html

>
>
> On Tuesday, May 21, 2013 11:13:12 AM UTC-7, Jeremiah Rounds wrote:
> > Hi random thought about Hive,
> >
> > Not to be assumed as a promise to do anything.
> >
> > We have been thinking lately about how to export data out of Rhipe into a data format that supports structured queries (SQL-like) for external collaboration.  Basically data comes into the Rhipe framework gets processes and goes out to other scientist who don't use hadoop.  We are torn as nothing seems "right sized".  The big problem is the data we want to export can be in the TB size, and propagating it into another technology via MapReduces requires concurrent writes, but none of the concurrent write data base technologies are something we want to support or really even have the expertise to be getting involved in.
> >
> > So I was thinking about Hive today which I think of as something in the middle.  Hive at least exposes an interface where non-hadoop scientist can write a query which gets translated into MapReduce and get data out.  It is not a particularly speedy sounding solution, but at least it takes the Rhipe writing analyst out of the loop for writing custom MapReduces to get the same data.
> >
> >
> >
> > Why the post though?
> >
> > I was looking at this post:
> > http://www.nearinfinity.com/blogs/stephen_mouring_jr/2013/01/04/writing-hive-tables-from-mapreduce.html
> >
> > Where the author points out that a MapReduce can read and write hive tables.  Which I thought was interesting because they didn't look all that complicated.   The data format that hive can handle is not as unstructured and expressive as a Rhipe, but if one steps back one can imagine a java class that takes rhcollect(NULL, matrix/data.frame) and translates it into hive format and vice-versa.   Potentially you could even jump back into a hive export, do your science with Rhipe, and jump back out with  a hive format output. i.e (input= rhfmt(..., type="hive", output=rhfmt(...,type="hive").  Thing is though the author points out that there is a step after the MapReduce where you have to tell hive about the update to a table, so I am not sure how practical that is if not used very carefully.
> >
> > I think it might be handy for that "jumping off" point where you leave the Rhipe pipe, and need to hand off to someone else.
> >
> > Obviously, I don't expect you to implement this, I was just brainstorming.
> >
> > Thanks.
> >

I agree with Saptarshi, always be suspicious of reading network folders on an actual cluster.  I have talked to IT support for a couple clusters before and they are always surprisingly okay with it, but it makes me nervous.  Hard to predict what kind of bottle-necking or denial of service or disk performance you will run into with reading from shared directories in MapReduce jobs.

You could zip up your jars and do a shared zip argument.  Check out rhwatch(..., shared="")

Shared itself is a thin wrapper for the hadoop DistributedCache system so it writes once per a node.
